Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Farmer
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark, Certain Songs: Certain songs
  Maladaptive Strategies: Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Avoid People: avoid other people, Avoid Sleep: Going to sleep or lying in the dark
  Memory: Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Vignette:
Sok was a 42-year-old married farmer from South Eastern Asia who had come to treatment after more than a year of living as if his mind and body had never fully come back from the night his young son nearly died. He described the illness as beginning innocently enough, with his child developing a fever that seemed ordinary at first, then worsening so quickly that the family was forced into the hospital in the middle of the night. Sok remembered the tube in his son’s mouth, the exposed skin of a small arm, the hospital lights washing everything pale and unreal, and the terrifying way his attention kept catching on specific body parts: the boy’s chest rising unevenly, his lips, his hands, the thinness of a leg that had gone slack. In those hours he had been certain that he was watching his child die in front of him, and even though the boy survived, Sok said the memory never settled into the past in the way other events did. Instead, when he remembered it, it came back with the force of something immediate and unfolding. He would suddenly see a fragment of the scene—an arm, a face, the angle of a bed rail—without warning, and the piece would arrive so abruptly that for a moment he felt pulled back into the hospital room before it vanished again.

In the months that followed, Sok became increasingly wary of the dark. Night-time had once been the time he returned from the fields, washed, ate with his family, and slept deeply beside his wife. After the illness, lying down after dark brought back the helplessness of the hospital and the fear that something terrible might happen again while everyone else slept. He began staying up very late, often until after the house had gone quiet and the night was nearly over, telling himself that if he stayed awake he would not have to lie in the dark with his thoughts. Even then, sleep felt risky. Going to bed meant having to turn off the light and lie still, and he found himself avoiding that moment whenever he could, lingering over chores, sitting outside longer than necessary, or checking on the house and yard in ways that gave him a little more time before he had to face the bed. On nights when he did wake in the dark, he would come awake sharply and feel the memory press in around him, as though the hospital had returned and his son might again be in danger.

Certain songs also became hard for him to hear. Sok could not predict exactly why a particular melody would strike him, but when one of those songs came on at a wedding, at a neighbor’s gathering, or drifting from a radio in the village, he felt his stomach tighten and his attention snap back to the time of the illness. What others experienced as background music seemed to him to carry the same atmosphere as those nights in the hospital, and he often left quietly or found an excuse to step away. Over time, this affected how he moved through daily life. As a farmer, Sok worked in an environment that was usually shared with others—neighbors passing by the fields, family members helping during busy seasons, people gathering after market days—but he had begun avoiding other people whenever he could. He turned down invitations, kept his distance at communal meals, and stayed focused on work rather than conversation. He said he did not want questions, and he did not trust himself not to become overwhelmed if someone mentioned sickness, children, or hospitals. The more he withdrew, the more his days narrowed to the practical tasks of farming and the private effort of getting through the hours until he could be alone again.

Despite his efforts, the memory did not remain contained. Sok described how pieces of it would appear suddenly and disappear just as fast, sometimes while he was working in the field, sometimes while standing in the dark at night, sometimes when a song caught him off guard. At those moments, he felt as if he were no longer remembering something finished but standing inside it again. He had come to believe that the event was never fully over, because his mind kept placing him back into it. What finally brought him in was the exhaustion of arranging his life around sleep, darkness, music, and other people, while still feeling hunted by a scene he could not keep at a distance. He said he wanted help because he was tired of living as though the hospital room were still waiting for him every night, and because he feared that if this continued, he would become even more cut off from his wife, his work, and the ordinary life he had before his son became ill.
